blocks.prompt: The Bug With a Spring in Its Knee
blocks.text: A grasshopper hatches from an egg in the ground. It looks like a tiny grasshopper with no wings. It eats grass and it grows. Soon its skin gets too tight, so it climbs out of that old skin and leaves it behind. It does this about five times. Then it has wings. A grasshopper does not hear with ears on its head. It hears with two flat spots on its belly. It has six legs, and the two back ones are the jumpers. Those legs stay folded and full of stored push, like a bent bow, waiting to go.

blocks.prompt: The Spring in the Knee
blocks.text:
A grasshopper can jump about twenty times the length of its own body. If you could do that, you would clear a school bus from a standing start.

Its muscles are not strong enough to do it. Muscles push slowly, and a jump like that needs a huge shove all at once. So the grasshopper cheats. Inside each back knee there is a small piece of springy stuff, a bit like rubber. The grasshopper locks its knee shut and pulls hard with its leg muscle. The muscle cannot open the locked knee, so all that pulling squeezes into the spring instead. The energy piles up and waits.

Then the lock lets go. The spring snaps back all at once, the leg kicks straight, and the grasshopper is in the air in less time than it takes you to blink. It is a catapult, not a push.

Grasshoppers do not hear with their heads. They have a thin round patch on each side of the belly that shivers when sound hits it. And they do not have two eyes. They have five.

answers: about twenty times its own body length

blocks.prompt: Every Grasshopper Carries a Catapult
blocks.text:
Watch a grasshopper launch and you are watching a machine that a person could not build out of muscle alone.

Here is the problem. A locust can throw itself a full meter, roughly twenty times its own body length, and it reaches full speed in about three hundredths of a second. Muscle cannot deliver power that fast. Muscle is strong but slow, like a person leaning on a heavy door. The jump needs the door to fly open in an instant.

So the grasshopper stores the push before it needs it. Each back leg holds a large muscle inside the thigh. Before the jump, the insect clamps the knee shut with a second, smaller muscle, and then the big muscle hauls with everything it has. The knee will not open. Instead the strain bends a curved band of hard shell at the joint and squeezes a pad of resilin, a natural rubber bouncier than most of the rubber we make. The leg is now a loaded bow.

Then the small muscle lets go. Everything stored comes out at once, the legs snap straight, and the grasshopper is gone.

Those same legs do a second job. A row of tiny pegs runs along the inside of each thigh. The grasshopper scrapes the pegs across a hard ridge on its wing, over and over, and the rasping song carries across a field. Another grasshopper hears it, not with ears on its head, but with a tight oval of skin on the side of its belly that trembles like the head of a drum.

blocks.prompt: The Quiet Insect That Becomes a Plague
blocks.text:
A desert locust is a grasshopper with a switch in it.

Most of the time it lives alone and wants to stay that way. It is pale green or sandy brown, matched to whatever it happens to be sitting on. It avoids other locusts. It eats, it hides, it keeps quiet. Scientists call this the solitary phase, and a solitary locust is one of the least alarming animals in the desert.

Then rain falls. Plants come up in scattered patches, and the young locusts that hatch are crowded onto those green patches together, bumping into one another all day long. The bumping is the trigger. When the hind legs of a locust are touched over and over, its nervous system floods with serotonin, a chemical it uses as a signal. Within a couple of hours the animal begins to change. It stops avoiding others and starts seeking them out. Within a generation or two, its young hatch yellow and black instead of green, with longer wings, broader shoulders, and larger brains. The loner has become a swarmer. Biologists call this the gregarious phase, and for a long time the two forms were filed as two separate species, because nobody could believe they were the same animal.

What follows is the oldest disaster in the written record. A swarm can cover hundreds of square kilometers and carry tens of millions of insects in every square kilometer of it. Each locust eats about its own weight in plants every day, which is roughly two grams, a number so small it sounds harmless. It is not. A swarm one square kilometer across eats as much food in a day as about thirty five thousand people.

And the switch runs backward. Keep a gregarious locust alone for long enough and it settles, fades back toward green, and forgets the crowd. The plague and the quiet insect in the grass are the same creature, waiting on the weather.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Rocky Mountain locust: Melanoplus spretus
Albert's Swarm, 1875: about 1,800 miles long
Estimated 3.5 trillion insects, the largest animal gathering ever recorded
Last living specimen collected in 1902
Catapult jump: cuticle band plus a resilin pad

blocks.prompt: Albert's Swarm: The Locust That Ate the Plains and Then Vanished
blocks.text:
In the summer of 1875, a doctor in Plattsmouth, Nebraska, named Albert Child did something nobody else had thought to do. A swarm of Rocky Mountain locusts was passing overhead, and instead of despairing at it, he measured it. He timed how long it took to pass. He telegraphed towns up and down the line to ask how wide the darkness was where they stood. Then he multiplied. His numbers described a living cloud roughly eighteen hundred miles long and one hundred and ten miles wide, holding, by later estimates, something like three and a half trillion insects. It remains the largest gathering of animals ever recorded on this planet, and it happened in living memory, over farmland, in front of witnesses.

To understand how an insect manages that, start with its knee. A locust cannot jump using muscle in the ordinary way, because muscle is strong but slow, and a jump demands enormous power inside a few thousandths of a second. So the animal cheats time. It locks the knee joint shut, contracts the great extensor muscle in its thigh against that lock, and pours the effort into a curved plate of hard cuticle and a pad of resilin, a rubbery protein springier than almost anything we manufacture. When the lock releases, everything stored leaves at once. The insect is a catapult that has learned to load itself.

Then there is the switch. A locust in ordinary times is a shy green loner. Crowd it and something remarkable happens: repeated touching of the hind legs floods its nervous system with serotonin, and within hours its behavior inverts. It seeks company instead of fleeing it. Its offspring hatch in warning colors, yellow and black, with longer wings and larger brains. For decades naturalists sorted the two forms into different species, because no one could accept that a hermit and a plague were the same animal wearing different clothes.

The Rocky Mountain locust had both tricks, the catapult and the crowd switch, and then it stopped. Swarms darkened the American West through the 1870s, stripping wheat, corn, wool off living sheep, and the wooden handles of tools where sweat had soaked in. By 1902 the last living specimen had been collected. Nobody killed them on purpose. Nobody could have. The insects were undone by geography. Their permanent home was the moist river valleys of the Rocky Mountains, a few hundred square miles of ground where they bred quietly between the great outbreaks. Settlers plowed those valleys, irrigated them, and grazed cattle across them, with no idea what they were doing, and the species that could blot out the sun across eighteen hundred miles could not survive the loss of a handful of sandy riverbanks.

That is the part worth sitting with. The Rocky Mountain locust was not rare, not fragile, not specialized in any way that looked dangerous. It was arguably the most abundant animal on the continent. It went extinct inside thirty years, by accident, because the small place it actually depended on was never the enormous place we saw it in.
